prompt: Has the Church replaced Israel?
answer:
Here is our working position on Israel and the end times. It is under review. It is not a settled Perazim doctrine, and we do not say every Christian must agree with it.

Jewish and Gentile believers are one New Covenant people in Christ (Ephesians 2:13–16). Jewish believers are part of the Church. Gentile believers are grafted into the blessings of God's promises (Romans 11:17–18), but they do not become ethnic Israelites. The Church has not replaced national Israel.

Our working position is pre-tribulation and premillennial, and it is under review. We understand that Christ will come for His Church before the tribulation (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18). Revelation 3:10 was addressed to the church in Philadelphia. Applying it to Christ's protection of His Church in the future tribulation is our working interpretation, supported by the other passages. The phrase "seven-year tribulation" is not in the text. Reading Daniel's final week (Daniel 9:24–27) as a future seven years is our working interpretation.

We understand that Christ will reign on earth for a thousand years (Revelation 20:1–6). Other passages help us understand that reign: Zechariah 14:4 and 14:9, Isaiah 11:1–10, and Daniel 2:34–35 and 2:44–45, where the stone becomes a great mountain and fills the earth. Connecting these with Christ's future physical reign on earth is our interpretation.

We understand that national Israel will turn to Jesus near the end of the tribulation (Romans 11:25–27; Zechariah 12:10). We connect this with Daniel 9:27, Daniel 12:1 and Matthew 24:15–22. This sequence is our interpretation. We do not set dates, and we do not identify any present-day person or nation as fulfilling these passages.

We understand the antichrist to be a final individual who opposes Christ and deceives people (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4; Daniel 7:8, 25). Revelation 13:1–8 describes the beast's blasphemy and war against the saints, and Revelation 13:11–14 describes its deception. We do not identify anyone today, and we do not guess.

The land was given and was possessed (Joshua 21:43), and God's covenant promises to Israel have not been cancelled (Romans 11:29). This is a covenant position, not a political endorsement. It does not mean that every action of any modern government is approved by God.

No one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36). Stay close to Scripture, and talk with your pastor.

Scripture:
Romans 11:25: “For I would not, brethren, that ye should be ignorant of this mystery, lest ye should be wise in your own conceits; that blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in.”
Revelation 3:10: “Because thou hast kept the word of my patience, I also will keep thee from the hour of temptation, which shall come upon all the world, to try them that dwell upon the earth.”

Connecting these with Christ's future physical reign on earth is our interpretation.

We understand that national Israel will turn to Jesus near the end of the tribulation (Romans 11:25–27; Zechariah 12:10). We connect this with Daniel 9:27, Daniel 12:1 and Matthew 24:15–22. Revelation 13:1–8 describes the beast's blasphemy and war against the saints, and Revelation 13:11–14 describes its deception. We do not identify anyone today, and we do not guess.

The land was given and was possessed (Joshua 21:43), and God's covenant promises to Israel have not been cancelled (Romans 11:29). This is a covenant position, not a political endorsement. It does not mean that every action of any modern government is approved by God.

answer:
Here is our working position on Israel and the end times. It is under review. It is not a settled Perazim doctrine, and we do not say every Christian must agree with it.

Jewish and Gentile believers are one New Covenant people in Christ (Ephesians 2:13–16). Jewish believers are part of the Church. Gentile believers are grafted into the blessings of God's promises (Romans 11:17–18), but they do not become ethnic Israelites. The Church has not replaced national Israel.

Our working position is pre-tribulation and premillennial, and it is under review. We understand that Christ will come for His Church before the tribulation (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18). Revelation 3:10 was addressed to the church in Philadelphia. Applying it to Christ's protection of His Church in the future tribulation is our working interpretation, supported by the other passages. The phrase "seven-year tribulation" is not in the text. Reading Daniel's final week (Daniel 9:24–27) as a future seven years is our working interpretation.

We understand that Christ will reign on earth for a thousand years (Revelation 20:1–6). Other passages help us understand that reign: Zechariah 14:4 and 14:9, Isaiah 11:1–10, and Daniel 2:34–35 and 2:44–45, where the stone becomes a great mountain and fills the earth. Connecting these with Christ's future physical reign on earth is our interpretation.

We understand that national Israel will turn to Jesus near the end of the tribulation (Romans 11:25–27; Zechariah 12:10). We connect this with Daniel 9:27, Daniel 12:1 and Matthew 24:15–22. This sequence is our interpretation. We do not set dates, and we do not identify any present-day person or nation as fulfilling these passages.

We understand the antichrist to be a final individual who opposes Christ and deceives people (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4; Daniel 7:8, 25). Revelation 13:1–8 describes the beast's blasphemy and war against the saints, and Revelation 13:11–14 describes its deception. We do not identify anyone today, and we do not guess.

The land was given and was possessed (Joshua 21:43), and God's covenant promises to Israel have not been cancelled (Romans 11:29). This is a covenant position, not a political endorsement. It does not mean that every action of any modern government is approved by God.

No one knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36). Stay close to Scripture, and talk with your pastor.

prompt: What do cessationists believe about the gifts of the Spirit?
answer:
Some cessationists teach that certain sign gifts, such as prophecy, healing and tongues, ceased with the apostolic age. Not every cessationist explains this in exactly the same way. This is a disagreement within Protestant Christianity.

Our position is that the gifts of the Holy Spirit continue to operate in the Church today. The Spirit gives gifts to each believer as He wills (1 Corinthians 12:7–11).

We weigh the view against these passages: Acts 2:38–39 (the promise is for us and our children) and Acts 2:17–18 (the last days, when God pours out His Spirit); 1 Corinthians 14:1 (desire spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy); Ephesians 4:11–13 (gifts given until the body is built up); and 1 Thessalonians 5:19–21 (do not quench the Spirit, and test everything).

Cessationists often read 1 Corinthians 13:8–10 as saying the gifts end when "that which is perfect" comes. Our reading, working interpretation and under review, is that this refers to the Lord's return and to full knowledge. We do not claim that the passage explicitly names the time as Christ's return, and we do not claim that this is the only possible reading.

We do not call cessationists heretics, false Christians or unsaved because they disagree. Test every word and experience by Scripture, desire the gifts that build up the Church, and seek love above all.

Scripture:
1 Corinthians 14:1: “Follow after charity, and desire spiritual gifts, but rather that ye may prophesy.”
Acts 2:39: “For the promise is unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off, even as many as the Lord our God shall call.”
